newsitem.title: UK: Fourth qtr demand can support air cargo surcharge.
newsitem.headline: Fourth qtr demand can support air cargo surcharge.

text.p: European airlines have led the way in the past week in introducing a cargo fuel surcharge, averaging around US 10 cents a kg reflecting a surge in jet fuel prices in recent months.
The action could have taken place earlier as airlines have been under pressure to improve their bottom line and combat yield erosion, air cargo industry sources said.
"But it is doubtful whether the market would have then been able to sustain the surcharge," one analyst added.
The rise in jet fuel costs is estimated by Germany's Lufthansa Cargo at 50 percent between July and October while Air France Cargo put the increase at 40 percent.

The fourth quarter is traditionally the strongest period for the air cargo business and this year there are also signs of economic recovery in key trading regions, giving a further fillip to trade, industry sources said.
"With demand strong and capacity limited -- at least for the next two months -- there is no doubt, the airlines can make the surcharge stick," said a London-based cargo manager.

Oil traders generally forecast a dip in prices from the present levels in the next two to three weeks. Over the winter as a whole, jet fuel is expected to remain firm or even strengthen if there is a very cold winter.
"But what happens if by January, fuel prices have come off and there is also extra cargo capacity ... customers will expect to benefit," one cargo analyst added.

"Even today (Friday) the question remains as to how far these surcharges will actually be applied. Major customers with long term contracts are likely to try to negotiate better terms, and they will probably be successful as no one wants to lose business in the present competitive climate," he said.

This week the International Air Transport Association (IATA) said it will hold an emergency Geneva meeting on November 13 to review the impact of higher fuel costs for passenger and cargo traffic on its 250 member airlines.
A spokesman said the average worldwide price of fuel paid by IATA members was U.S.73.9 cents per U.S. gallon in the first nine months of this year, against U.S. 65.2 cents in 1995.
Other airlines which have announced cargo surcharges include British Airways Plc, KLM Royal Dutch Airlines Virgin Atlantic, while Swissair is introducing a rate increase.

Airlines operating from Hong Kong to Europe will be applying a surcharge and this is also likely to be introduced for trans-Pacific routes, the chief executive of Hong Kong's cargo airline, Air Hong Kong Ltd, Stanley Hui said.

So far the major North American airlines have not yet made public any decision, with some industry sources suggesting there may be a tacit agreement not to announce any surcharges just before the U.S. presidential election on November 5.

"But there is also a practical aspect as billing and accounting software has to be adapted to cope with the surcharge, and that can't take place overnight," a cargo manager for a U.S. airline said on Friday. --Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax +44 171 542 5017
